html:
A small fan-shaped artificial island in the harbour of Nagasaki, built in 1634 to 1636. From 1641 to 1859 it was the only place where Europeans could trade with Japan, and the only Europeans allowed were the Dutch.

It was built to hold the Portuguese, to keep them and their Christianity apart from the people. After the Shimabara Rebellion the Portuguese were expelled in 1639, and in 1641 the Dutch East India Company was moved here from Hirado. The Dutch had shown they cared about trade, not converts.

The island was about 120 by 75 metres, joined to the city by one guarded bridge. A handful of Dutch staff lived there and traded copper, silver and later porcelain for silk, sugar, books and goods from Asia. Each year the head of the post travelled to Edo to see the shogun.

Through Dejima came Western books on medicine, astronomy and science, the base of Dutch learning in Japan, seen in works like the Kaitai Shinsho. The post lost its role when Japan opened its ports in the 1850s.
